title: Egypt moved the temples of Abu Simbel out of the Nile's reach
body: A new dam threatened to submerge Egypt's Abu Simbel temples. An international project backed by UNESCO moved them to higher ground, where the reconstructed site opened on 22 September 1968.
takeaway: Saving a monument can mean recreating the cliff that once held it as well as moving the stonework.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Working Together: Abu Simbel
visual: a colossal seated stone figure at Abu Simbel framed by a sandstone cliff

title: A 10-metre wall at Great Zimbabwe stands without mortar
body: At Great Zimbabwe, a city built by ancestors of the Shona, the Great Enclosure has an outer wall about 10 metres high and up to 5 metres thick. Builders laid its granite blocks in courses without mortar to bind them.
takeaway: The wall itself preserves evidence of how southern African builders shaped and stacked stone centuries ago.
source: Smithsonian Institution, Great Enclosure archive and The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Great Zimbabwe
visual: the curved outer wall of the Great Enclosure at Great Zimbabwe with shallow light catching the granite courses

title: A pipe lets Lake Nyos release gas a little at a time
body: At Lake Nyos in Cameroon, carbon dioxide builds up in deep water. In 2001 engineers began removing it through a pipe. Once the water starts rising, some of its gas comes out of solution and helps keep the flow going.
takeaway: The same tendency that makes gas come out of rising water can help control how quickly it escapes.
source: US Geological Survey, Degassing Lakes Nyos and Monoun (2005)
visual: a slender fountain from an unmarked pipe near the centre of a quiet crater lake
